items.title: Akiyoshi Toshiko — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: Max [Roach] would let me sit in

ctx.x: I think what I‟m trying to highlight here is that you‟re composing, so, several compositions, but we‟ll talk about that later in the interview, your process of composition, et cetera. But the fact that, you know, you have several originals on this session, so….

Yeah, right. I think it‟s, I started writing because, when I came to Boston I used to, of course, I used to go every night to listen, and in those days like, uh, even the big bands, like Duke‟s band or Basie‟s band, would stay for two weeks, you know, at a club. You can‟t think of that today, but…. I was always sitting in, I decided that when I, if somebody asked me to sit in, I was going to sit in. You know, I decided that. So, I used to sit in with, Max [Roach] would let me sit in, Miles would let me sit in, so…
Was your experience at Berklee, did it, um, uh … highlight or advance this compositional impetus of yours? Did it help you in any way, or…?

items.title: Toshiko Akiyoshi interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 17, 1999
items.q: Later he was, in a short time he was with Max Roach’s group.

ctx.x: No, nothing. So you learn that way. And there’s another very precious lesson in those days, were drafted musicians from here, professional ones, some of them noteworthy like Hampton Hawes for example that’s a noted player. Even those not that noted, Eddie Costa. There was a drum player, later he was playing with Eddie’s group or somebody like that. But anyway, there were quite many good players in Japan in the Army and, not Navy, but Air Force band. And they would come and sit in where I had my own group. And I…
Did you start writing them down, or did they just become memorized immediately yourself?
